explanation: An empty map has no buckets; the first insertion creates 8. Inserting an existing key changes nothing. insert copies the key and the value; try_emplace moves the key and builds the value in place; operator[] of a new key copies the key and default-constructs the value (0). Each element is one heap block, plus one for the bucket array.

The ninth insertion would make size() > bucket_count(), so the table doubles to 16 buckets. Rehashing relinks the existing nodes: no key or value is copied or moved (copies() goes up only by the 2 of the new element), and key 8 now lives in bucket 8 % 16 = 8.
With hash mode 1 every key hashes to 0, so all elements share bucket 0's chain. Lookups must compare keys with KeyEqual, and erase must unlink correctly wherever the element is in the chain.
Lookups, erase and copies of a map with no buckets must not divide by zero or allocate.
Inserting a key that is already present never grows the table and never copies or moves anything.
rehash relinks every node into the bucket hash % bucket_count() of the new table, which need not be a power of two; no element is copied, moved or reallocated.
rehash(n) grows to max(n, size()) buckets only if that is more than now; it never shrinks.
After rehash(3) the table doubles from 3 to 6 when the fourth element arrives.
Erasing from one long chain: the head, the tail and the middle, then everything.
Erase destroys the key and the value and frees the node; the bucket count stays.
operator[] inserts a default-constructed value for a new key (copying or moving the key) and returns the existing value otherwise.
try_emplace leaves its key argument untouched when the key is present, and forwards its arguments to build the value in place.
clear destroys every element and frees the nodes but keeps the buckets.
A copy has the same bucket count, copies each key and value once, and is independent.
Copy assignment destroys the target's elements and gives it copies of the source's, with the source's bucket count.
m = m must leave m unchanged.
Moving a map takes over its buckets and nodes without touching any element; the source is left empty with no buckets, and is still usable.
m = std::move(m) must leave m unchanged.
The destructor destroys every element once and frees every node and the bucket array.
